Lessons.Title: More Nets, More Surface Area
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Construct foldable prism/pyramid nets, use their polygons to calculate surface area, and distinguish surface usage from the number of unit cubes a box holds.

A polyhedron net must show each outside face exactly once, with correctly connected matching edges. A triangular prism has two matching triangles and three lateral rectangles. A square pyramid has one square and four triangular faces. Label the faces with lengths and right-angle heights before finding their areas.

Different rectangular boxes can have equal cubic-unit capacity yet require different amounts of wrapping or cardboard. Compare surface area as area, not volume. A net or student-built original polyhedron needs teacher review of face connections, validity and explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Foldable face-adjacency net
KeyConcepts.Definition: A net is a planar layout of every outer polygon of a solid, connected to reproduce its edges when folded.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Draw every face, match shared-edge lengths, and check no folded overlap.
KeyConcepts.Example: A triangular prism includes two congruent triangles and three rectangles.

KeyConcepts.Title: Net surface area
KeyConcepts.Definition: The total two-dimensional exterior of a solid equals the sum of the areas in any valid net.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add every face exactly once in square units.
KeyConcepts.Example: A triangular prism with 3–4–5 end triangles and length 6 has area 2×6 + 6(3+4+5)=84 square centimeters.

KeyConcepts.Title: Surface versus capacity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Surface area measures material for an outside shell; volume measures enclosed unit cubes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Calculate both independently when comparing boxes, with area in cm² and volume in cm³.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 2×3×6 and a 3×3×4 box both hold 36 cm³ but have surface areas 72 cm² and 66 cm².

WorkedExamples.Title: Net of a triangular prism
WorkedExamples.Question: A triangular-prism base is a right triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 cm, and the prism is 6 cm long. Find exterior area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Enumerate the two triangular bases and three rectangles in a valid net.
Steps: Each right triangle area is 3×4÷2=6 cm²; both total 12 cm².
Lateral rectangle areas are 3×6=18, 4×6=24, and 5×6=30 cm².
Total net area is 12+18+24+30=84 cm².
Verify all five faces connect along matching edge lengths and fold into the prism.
WorkedExamples.Check: The two triangle bases and all three lateral faces must each be counted once.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare surface and capacity of two boxes
WorkedExamples.Question: Which uses less cardboard: a closed 2×3×6 cm prism or a closed 3×3×4 cm prism, and which contains more unit cubes?
WorkedExamples.Method: Calculate external face areas and volumes separately.
Steps: Both volumes are 36 cm³, as 2×3×6=3×3×4=36.
Conclude B uses 6 cm² less material but has equal ideal cubic capacity.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Box B uses less cardboard (66 vs 72 cm²), and both hold 36 cm³.
WorkedExamples.Check: Neither conclusion follows solely from the other statistic; calculate both.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct an original polyhedron net
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw a foldable triangular-prism or square-pyramid net with all face lengths labeled, then compare it with a peer's different net of the same solid.
WorkedExamples.Method: Teacher-reviewed drawing and explanation with a face inventory.
Steps: Name the solid and list the required polygon faces.
Draw a connected net with matched shared edges and dimensions.
Explain how every face folds to the solid without overlap.
Calculate total area and compare with another valid net.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Multiple valid nets can exist for the same solid, but they must represent the same faces and surface area.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher or peer validates polygon count, connection, dimension scale and geometric justification; a single numeric result cannot prove foldability.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using all correct polygons but attaching faces along incompatible edges.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The resulting planar drawing cannot fold into the intended solid without overlap or mismatch.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the solid's actual face adjacency and match shared-edge lengths in the net.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming that equal box volumes require equal amounts of cardboard.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A change of dimensions can alter total face areas without changing the three-dimensional product.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compute area and volume separately in different units and compare the two outputs.

SummaryPoints: A valid net contains all outer faces, with matched edges and connections.
Add polygonal face areas in square units; volume describes cubic-unit capacity.
Drawn nets require teacher review for foldability beyond correct arithmetic.

Visuals.Title: Prism net faces and box comparisons
Visuals.Description: Text-accessible original net plan: two right triangles with side lengths 3,4,5 cm and three attached rectangles of dimensions 3-by-6,4-by-6,5-by-6 cm. Their areas total 84 cm². Separately compare a 2-by-3-by-6 box (area 72, volume 36) and a 3-by-3-by-4 box (area 66, volume 36); all lengths in centimeters.
Visuals.SecondaryLabel: Equal volume 36 cm³, areas 72 and 66 cm²

Lessons.Title: Distinguishing Between Surface Area and Volume
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Compare length, surface area and volume with appropriate dimensions, and construct examples showing these are independent attributes.

Length counts one-dimensional distance. Surface area counts exposed outside unit squares, including faces hidden from a viewer. Volume counts the enclosed three-dimensional unit cubes. The units themselves reveal the difference: cm, cm² and cm³ are not interchangeable.

Build two different solids from eight unit cubes; both have volume 8 but can have different surface areas. In reverse, a 1-by-1-by-5 prism and a 1-by-2-by-3 prism both expose 22 square units but enclose 5 and 6 cubic units, respectively.

Original student designs can be non-prisms; their unit-cube count still determines volume while a systematic count of externally exposed faces determines surface area. Teacher reviews visual constructions, not only the final numbers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Three measurement dimensions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Length, area and volume respectively measure one-, two- and three-dimensional quantities.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Write corresponding linear, square and cubic units.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 2-cm edge has length 2 cm; a 2-by-3 face has area 6 cm²; a 2-by-3-by-4 prism has volume 24 cm³.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same volume, different exposure
KeyConcepts.Definition: The arrangement of a fixed set of unit cubes changes contact faces and exposed surface.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Volume equals cube count; count only outside square faces for surface area.
KeyConcepts.Example: Eight cubes arranged 2×2×2 expose 24 squares; arranged 1×1×8 expose 34 squares.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same area, different capacity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two geometric solids may have identical total outside face areas but unequal volumes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For a rectangular prism, calculate 2(ab+bc+ac) and abc independently.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 1×1×5 prism has area 22 and volume 5; a 1×2×3 prism has area 22 and volume 6.

WorkedExamples.Title: Eight cubes with changing surface
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare a 2×2×2 cube, a 1×2×4 prism, and a 1×1×8 prism, each built from eight unit cubes.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count unit-cube volume and six outer face regions for each design.
Steps: All three volumes are 8 cubic units.
The 2×2×2 cube exposes 6×4=24 square units.
The 1×2×4 prism exposes 2(2+4+8)=28 square units.
The 1×1×8 prism exposes 2(1+8+8)=34 square units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: All volumes are 8, while surface areas are 24, 28 and 34 square units.
WorkedExamples.Check: None of the touching internal cube faces are counted as exposed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Same area but unequal volumes
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare closed rectangular prisms of dimensions 1×1×5 and 1×2×3 centimeters.
Steps: Prism A surface is 2(1+5+5)=22 cm².
Prism B surface is 2(2+3+6)=22 cm².
Prism A volume is 1×1×5=5 cm³.
Prism B volume is 1×2×3=6 cm³.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both expose 22 cm², but their volumes differ: 5 cm³ versus 6 cm³.
WorkedExamples.Check: Equal square area does not imply equal cubic capacity.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build and defend two original eight-cube shapes
WorkedExamples.Question: Design two different connected solids each with eight unit cubes, including a nonrectangular arrangement if desired. Measure their exterior face areas.
WorkedExamples.Method: Student-selected building/diagram task with teacher-reviewed complete face accounting.
Steps: Create two labeled distinct assemblies, using eight unit cubes in each.
Count each body's unit cubes to confirm volume 8.
Mark and count exterior unit squares systematically, including hidden faces.
Compare areas, explain internal cube contacts, and invite peer feedback.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Many valid constructions exist; both have volume 8 while the outside areas may match or differ.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks physically feasible connection, no overlapping cubes, correct external face counting and clear area-versus-volume explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming identical volumes imply equal surface areas.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Changing cube adjacency changes how many unit-square faces are exposed.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compute surface from all outer faces separately from volume.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming identical surface areas imply identical volumes.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two prisms can have the same surface 22 cm² while enclosing 5 or 6 cm³.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Including the hidden internal faces where unit cubes meet.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Contact faces are not on the outside surface of the assembly.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count faces visible from every outside direction, not faces touching another cube.

SummaryPoints: Length uses linear units, outside area square units and occupied volume cubic units.
Fixed eight-cube count gives equal volume but possibly different exterior area.
Equal exterior area can also coexist with different volumes; original cube constructions require human review.

Visuals.Title: Independent measures in cube-built shapes
Visuals.Description: Text-accessible independent diagram specification: three solids each using eight identical unit cubes, arranged as 2-by-2-by-2 (outside area 24), 1-by-2-by-4 (area 28), and 1-by-1-by-8 (area 34). A separate pair of prisms 1-by-1-by-5 and 1-by-2-by-3 have the same outside surface area 22 square units but volumes 5 and 6 cubic units. Exclude internal touching faces.
